                                                    COMMENTS

           Texas Electric Cooperatives, Inc. (TEC) respectfully submits these comments in response

to the Public Utility Commission of Texas (Commission) Staff’s (Staff) request for comments

regarding the proposal for publication (PFP) to update wholesale and investor owned utility (IOU)

retail transmission cost recovery within ERCOT.1 TEC is the statewide association of electric

cooperatives operating in Texas, representing its members except as their interests may be

separately represented.2 The PFP directs comments to be filed by August 11, 2026. These

comments are timely filed.

                                              I.    Staff Questions

1.         Should the values associated with the large load minimum billing demand provisions
           be different for large load customers with different contracted peak demands or
           different non-coincident (NCP) demands?

           Based on the newly proposed minimum billing demand charges proposed by Commission

Staff, TEC expects the values associated with large load minimum billing demand will differ

anyway, without separate provisions for types of large load customers.3 As long as the different

minimum billing demand values are related to usage and demands placed on the bulk electric

system, the values would be different and not uniform across large loads.

2.         Should the large load minimum billing demand be:

           a.      fixed for 20 years as proposed;

           b.      reduced in phases over a period of 20 years; or




1
    Staff Memo w/MS Word version of PFP approved by the Commission at 07.09 OM (Jul. 10, 2026) (PFP).
2
  TEC’s 78 members include distribution cooperatives that provide retail electric utility service to approximately
5,000,000 consumers in statutorily authorized service areas that encompass more than half of the total area of the state.
TEC’s G&T members generally acquire generation resources and power supply for their member distribution
cooperatives and deliver electricity to them at wholesale.
3

                                                           2
        c.      extended to a longer time period?

       TEC recommends that the duration of the large load billing demand be linked to the life of

the load rather than a set timeframe. This is a reasonable mechanism for large loads to pay for the

burden they place on the system. There is no guarantee that a load will exist for 20 years. A load

that does not exist for 20 years will not pay the minimum billing demand for a pre-set 20-year

timeframe, potentially undermining how costs are spread among ratepayers if all large load cost

share is based on a 20-year period. Moreover, a large load that exists beyond 20 years continues

to place a high burden on the system and should be required to ensure that other ratepayers are not

subsidizing its usage beyond 20 years. A minimum billing demand that is linked to the life of the

load ensures cost recovery from those that cause the costs over the period the costs are incurred.

3.     Should the large load minimum billing demand be based on some measure of demand
       lower than contracted peak demand and NCP demand? For example, should the large
       load minimum billing demand:

       a.      reflect a “ratcheted” demand, wherein the large load minimum billing demand
               is some percentage of the customer’s contracted peak demand or maximum
               NCP demand in the previous year? If so, should the ratchet percentage decline
               in phases over the years, and how?

       b.      be based on a “weighted average” minimum billing demand, wherein the large
               load minimum billing demand is some weighted average of the large load
               customer’s contracted peak demand or highest NCP demand over the previous
               year and the large load customer’s 12CP demand? If so, should the percentage
               weighting towards contracted peak demand or NCP demand decline in phases
               over the years, and how?

       TEC recommends that the large load minimum billing demand be based on the large load’s

contracted peak demand with no reduction, ratcheting, or weighting. The electric system is being

built to serve the projected load demands based on contracted peak amounts. The contract will

limit the maximum demand, which should be tied to the amount of load approved for

interconnection. The projected amounts of demand on a systemwide basis are therefore most

closely aligned with contracted peak demand. Therefore, the minimum billing demand should



                                                 3
 track contracted peak demand. To do otherwise would inappropriately shift the costs of

construction of the electric system to serve large loads to other loads that are not the cause of the

needed construction.

4.     Should separate rate treatment be applied to a large computational load, defined as
       an entity that is subject to §25.194 of this title (relating to Large Load Interconnection
       Standards) and in which 50% or greater of the demand at the site consists of power
       electronic based load, specifically computational load, such as data centers and
       cryptocurrency mining facilities? Responses to this question should include
       applicable legal support or limitations regarding separate rate treatment for large
       computational loads.

       No comment at this time.

5.     Should the definition for transmission interconnection costs be broadened to include
       transmission projects that are recommended at the conclusion of a batch study to
       serve the transmission capacity needs of a particular load?

       At a high level, transmission costs driven directly by the interconnection of large loads

should be allocated to those loads. However, in practice, system improvements that result from a

batch analysis may be difficult to quantify and directly assign to a particular load. As TEC

understands the new batch study process, the results of the batch study will result in actionable

transmission plans. If there are projects within the actionable plan that can be specifically

associated with a single load, these costs should be assigned directly to that load. Assuming it can

be proven that a single load or loads are driving the need for a project, and this project does not

result in benefits to the system at large, costs associated with these batch study transmission

projects that are paid for by a large load should not be included in a transmission service provider’s

(TSP) transmission cost of service (TCOS) or transmission service rates paid by all other ERCOT

ratepayers. TEC notes that it will be difficult to quantify, in some cases, which transmission

projects are caused solely by a particular large load because projects will be analyzed

simultaneously in a batch.




                                                  4
            Transmission interconnection costs, under the proposed PFP language, will be specifically

excluded from TCOS.4 Broadening the definition of transmission interconnection costs to include

the costs of proposed batch study projects that are needed to serve specific loads will prevent such

costs from being socialized to other ratepayers through TCOS.

           Allocating to large loads identifiable costs associated with specific projects follows cost

causation principles, if such costs are caused by the large loads that applied for the large load

interconnections. Governor Abbott specifically directed the Commission to protect residential

ratepayers from large load infrastructure costs, require large loads to fully fund the cost of

infrastructure needed to service their operations, and reduce residential ratepayer’s transmission

costs.5 Broadening the definition of transmission interconnection costs to include transmission

projects that are recommended at the conclusion of a batch study may align with the Governor’s

directive at a high level.

           However, projects that support the system at large must remain eligible for recovery

through TCOS. Unless another mechanism is developed to make whole neighboring TSPs, any

required upgrades associated with a batch study project should be recoverable if not paid for by

the interconnecting large load. A policy that disallows the recovery of costs associated with

projects that provide a system-wide benefit would be a significant deviation from the current policy

of socializing costs associated with transmission upgrades that provide broader system benefits.

Ultimately, native load may also benefit from projects produced by a batch analysis.

6.         If a large load customer is able to reserve transmission capacity irrespective of
           whether the large load customer has energized or is fully using available capacity,
           how should these loads be reflected in the resource adequacy reports and assessments
           and transmission planning studies?


4

5

                                  II.    General Comments

       TEC’s member cooperatives represent a diverse set of load profiles across the state, with

varying degrees of traditional industrial load, computational large load, and smaller residential or

commercial loads. Because of these different profiles, moving from a 4 coincident peak (CP)

determinant with fifteen-minute intervals to a 12CP determinant with thirty-minute intervals will

impact TEC’s member cooperatives in different ways. TEC, therefore, takes no position on the

transition to a 12CP methodology with thirty-minute intervals. An increased number of CPs and

increased interval length may lessen the likelihood that large load consumers can avoid

transmission costs but may increase costs for some TEC members. Efficient market signals are

vital to maintaining appropriate levels of generation and transmission buildout. Ultimately,

regardless of the methodology chosen, whether that be a set number of CPs, net CPs, or total

system usage, the Commission should endeavor to adopt a methodology that minimizes distortions

to the energy market.

       Following adoption of the new transmission cost allocation methodology, the Commission

should continue to periodically monitor transmission cost allocation as more sophisticated users

adjust to the new CP regime, increasing their ability to potentially avoid CPs and shift costs onto

other consumers.

                                  III.   §25.192 Comments

A.     Definitions

       1.      Revise transmission interconnection costs definition




                                                 6
            First, the proposed definition of “transmission interconnection costs”6 should be clarified

to include only costs associated with large load customers. As currently written, the definition does

not include a reference to large loads and could be interpreted to apply to any transmission

interconnection costs, which is inconsistent with the Legislature’s mandate in Senate Bill 6 of the

89th Regular Session.

           Second, if transmission costs can be directly associated with a project driven by a specific

large load and the benefits of the project will accrue only to the large load, these costs should be

included in the definition of transmission interconnection costs. As noted previously, this

expansion should not include associated projects for neighboring but not interconnecting TSPs

required to upgrade their systems to accommodate a batch study project, unless a new mechanism

is developed to ensure that these TSPs are also made whole by the interconnecting large load or

are granted a direct and enforceable right to recover costs from the interconnecting large load.

Further, if transmission projects benefit the system at large, related costs should continue to be

socialized consistent with current Commission practice.

           TEC therefore proposes the following edits to the definition of transmission

interconnection costs at §25.192(b)(13):

           (13)    Transmission interconnection costs -- All costs associated with the

           facilities required to physically interconnect or upgrade the interconnection of a

           transmission-level large load customer, or a distinct set of transmission-level large

           load customers, to the existing transmission network, including interconnection

           lines, substation additions or modifications, and associated equipment necessary to

           establish or modify service, and transmission projects recommended at the


6
    PFP at 12 (proposed §25.192(b)(13)).




                                                    7
            conclusion of a batch study to serve the transmission capacity needs of a particular

           large load customer, if it can be determined these projects do not provide system

           benefits. This term does not include transmission projects recommended at the

           conclusion of a batch study associated with non-interconnecting transmission

           service providers, unless those costs are paid for by the interconnecting large load

           customer or subject to a right of recovery.

           2.      Revise wholesale transmission service at distribution voltage rate definition

           TEC recommends a minor change to the definition of wholesale transmission service at

distribution voltage (WTSDV) rate, which currently refers to a rate “established by the

Commission.”7 The Commission cannot “establish” a WTSDV rate for an electric cooperative.

The electric cooperative’s board has “exclusive jurisdiction” to “set all terms of access, conditions,

and rates applicable to services provided by the electric cooperative . . . including

nondiscriminatory and comparable rates for distribution.”8 A WTSDV rate is for the use of

distribution facilities, not transmission facilities.

           The Commission has limited jurisdiction over electric cooperatives. 9 The Commission’s

role with respect to an electric cooperative’s WTSDV rate is largely an oversight role10 limited to

ensuring open access and comparable terms pursuant to PURA § 35.004(a).11 Thus, the

Commission does not set or establish this rate in the first instance, but rather reviews the rate set

framework, TEC recommends deleting the words “transmission” and “established by the

                   transmission rate for a TSP or DSP established by the Commission to

                   to provide wholesale transmission service at distribution voltage.

           3.      Conform the non-IOU DSP and non-IOU TSP definitions and entity
                   terminology

           The PFP introduces two new defined terms — “non-investor-owned utility distribution

service provider (non-IOU DSP)” and “non-investor-owned utility transmission service provider

(non-IOU TSP)” — at §25.192(b)(10) and (11). These terms carry significant weight: later

provisions use them to determine which entities bear obligations and which receive protections.

Currently, Chapter 25 does not use the abbreviation “IOU,” and it refers to these entities as “non-

investor-owned transmission service providers” — the phrasing in §25.247, which schedules the

same entities into proceedings under §25.192(g) and (h). The added word “utility” also sits in

tension with PURA’s defined term “electric utility,” which excludes municipally owned utilities,

denied).
13

                                                      9
 electric cooperatives, and river authorities. TEC recommends conforming the new labels to the

Commission’s existing usage:

           (10)   Non-investor-owned utility distribution service provider (non-IOU

           DSP) -- A DSP that is a municipally owned utility, river authority, or electric

           cooperative.

           (11)   Non-investor-owned utility transmission service provider (non-IOU

           TSP) -- A TSP that is a municipally owned utility, river authority, or electric

           cooperative.

           Relatedly, the PFP uses IOU, non-IOU, TSP, DSP, and IOU DSP inconsistently, and in

several places says “DSP” where the substance plainly reaches only IOU DSPs. Each instance may

be minor standing alone; however, together they create a risk that an electric cooperative or

municipally owned utility is pulled into an investor-owned-utility-specific obligation by imprecise

drafting rather than by design — and that risk is highest in precisely the provisions where the

Commission drew jurisdictional lines. TEC requests that the Commission conform entity

terminology throughout §§25.192, 25.193, and 25.252 and apply each defined term consistently

with the applicability the Commission intends.

B.         Separate WTSDV tariffs and TCOS proceedings

           Proposed §25.192(c)(2) would require a TSP to include “a separate section to reflect

wholesale transmission service at distribution voltage rates, terms, and conditions set by the

commission.”14 TEC urges the Commission to reject this proposition, at least for electric

cooperatives and municipally owned utilities.




14
     PFP at 13.




                                                 10
           First, as explained above, the Commission does not have jurisdiction to “set” the rate for

WTSDV provided by an electric cooperative.15 Second, WTSDV rates are distinct and separate

from wholesale transmission service rates.16 Distribution-level wholesale service is not an element

of TCOS. Rule 25.192 only allows for the recovery of transmission costs and specifically limits

those costs to expenses and investment recorded in transmission-related Federal Energy

Regulatory Commission (FERC) accounts,17 while WTSDV tariffs under 16 TAC § 25.191 allow

for the recovery of distribution costs that are recorded in separate FERC accounts for distribution

expense and investment.18 Accordingly, when a utility provides wholesale service using

distribution facilities, it does so under a dedicated WTSDV tariff because distribution-level service

is carved out from TCOS charges.

          Commission precedent consistently reflects this separation.19 In Docket No. 51606, for

example, the Commission noted that “[a] tariff for wholesale transmission service at distribution

voltage under 16 TAC § 25.191 differs from a tariff for transmission service under 16 TAC

§ 25.192.”20 It is due to this difference that Staff reasoned in Docket No. 51606 that “[c]osts not

           Commission Staff’s proposed inclusion of WTSDV in §25.192(c)(2) would expand the

scope of TCOS proceedings in a manner that conflicts with PURA, Texas Supreme Court

precedent,22 and Commission precedent. Accordingly, the Commission should continue to employ

a separate tariff filing for WTSDV rates, with the rate initially set by the electric cooperative’s

board of directors. TEC recommends revising §25.192(c)(2) to recognize the statutory framework

and exclusive jurisdiction applicable to electric cooperatives and municipally owned utilities in

establishing WTSDV tariffs, as follows:

           (2) If the TSP provides wholesale transmission service at distribution voltage, the

           tariff required by this section must include the TSP must file a separate section tariff

           to reflect wholesale transmission service at distribution voltage rates, terms, and

           conditions set by the commission, the regulatory authority of a municipally owned

           utility, or the board of directors of an electric cooperative, as applicable. A TSP

           must file an application to establish such tariff within 30 days of receiving a request

           for such service.

C.         Changes to DSP and ERCOT 12CP values should be subject to notice and hearing

           Proposed §25.192(f)(1) states in part: “The commission may approve changes to DSP

12CP values and the ERCOT 12CP value at any time.”23 The existing rule at 16 TAC § 25.192(d)

does not contemplate that the Commission can change the 4CP values at any time. A DSP’s billing

units and the ERCOT average 4CP are established in a contested case proceeding initiated by

22
     See Tex. Mun. Power Agency v. Pub. Util. Comm’n of Texas, 253 S.W.3d 184, 194 (Tex. 2007).
23

                                                         12
 Commission Staff upon notice to DSPs.24 DSPs are thus given notice and an opportunity for

hearing to ensure the billing units are accurate.

           TEC is concerned that the Commission’s proposed ability to change the 12CP values at

any time will invite regulatory uncertainty, billing chaos, and market disruption, if changes are not

subject to notice and an opportunity for hearing. Market participants need advance notice, the

ability to evaluate the basis for any change, and time to plan for changes in billing units and cost

allocation. While sudden, ad hoc changes may not be Commission Staff’s intention, the current

language is unrestricted and concerning for market participants. TEC recommends the following

changes to proposed §25.192(f)(1) to give more certainty to the market:

           Following notice and an opportunity for hearing, theThe Commission may approve

           changes to DSP 12CP values and the ERCOT 12CP value at any time.

D.         Allow non-IOU DSPs to report settlement-quality meter data through TSP or TO

           Proposed §25.192(f)(1)(A) requires non-IOU DSPs to provide ERCOT “timely access to

settlement-quality meter data for each large load customer in its service territory.”25 TEC members

do not object to sharing or providing access to such data, but the manner of access requires

additional consideration. Distribution-only electric cooperatives may not frequently interact with

or share data directly with ERCOT. The communication or provision of data likely occurs through

their TSP or transmission operator (TO). Accordingly, TEC requests that DSPs be permitted to

share settlement-quality meter data with ERCOT through their designated TSP or TO.

            TEC further notes that “timely” is an undefined, vague term. The rule specifies no time

interval or submission frequency for the submission of settlement-quality data. TEC requests

clarification regarding what constitutes “timely access.”

           The ERCOT Protocols already define settlement-quality meter data and are the appropriate

location for these mechanics. Second, settlement-quality metering may not exist today at every

large load site served by a non-IOU DSP, because many distribution cooperatives’ large loads are

metered on the transmission side. Compliance will be affected by equipment, cost, and lead-times.

The Protocols should accordingly establish an implementation timeline.

           Moreover, TEC recommends further clarification to this section to address the situation in

which a large load customer may be located within a DSP’s service territory that is multiply

certificated to other DSPs. A DSP should only be required to provide access to meter data for large

loads to which it is providing service. Accordingly, TEC recommends the following changes to

proposed §25.192(f)(1)(A):

           (A)    A Nnon-IOU DSPs must provide ERCOT, directly or through its designated

                  TSP or transmission operator, timely access to settlement-quality meter data

                  for each large load customer it serves within its service territory.

E.         Clarify when ERCOT will perform adjustments to 12CP load values

           Proposed §25.192(f)(1)(B) requires ERCOT to perform adjustments to each DSP 12CP

load value to account for large load demands.26 Consistent with its comments above regarding ad

hoc changes to 12CP values at any time, TEC recommends that the rule provide clarity regarding

when or how frequently these adjustments will occur.




26
     PFP at 18.

 F.         Remove duplicate ability of Commission to require TSP to file application to revise
           rates

           Proposed §25.192(i) states in part that “The commission may, at any time, require a TSP

to file an application to revise its rates.” This sentence duplicates the authority already stated in 16

TAC §25.247(b)(5) and (d)(2), which applies to both investor-owned electric utilities and non-

investor-owned TSPs. Importantly, the existing language in §25.247 conditions the Commission’s

initiation of a rate proceeding on “the basis of other criteria that the commission determines are in

the public interest, including but not limited to the information provided in [an]. . . earnings

monitoring report.”27 Under proposed new §25.192(i), the Commission would have unbounded

authority to require a TSP to file an application to revise its rates at any time and for no reason.28

While TEC understands the need to require a TSP to update its rates, there should be a public

interest basis for the requirement, given the time and cost associated with comprehensive rate

proceedings. TEC recommends deleting this sentence or revising it to align with the existing

language in §25.247.

G.         Over-recovery refunds

           While proposed §25.192(j)(3) largely tracks the existing rule, the PFP proposes a new

sentence at the end of the section that would give the Commission the ability to order a compliance

proceeding to determine the final amounts of over-recovery that must be refunded to customers

and the form of the refund.29 TEC is not opposed to a compliance proceeding but has concerns

regarding the ability of the Commission to order the form of a refund. TSPs may use different

methods to return refunds to DSPs, whether in the form of a direct payment or bill credits, and

 should be afforded this flexibility. What is more important is the timing of the refund: when it

must ultimately be done and whether in a single payment or series of payments over a defined

                   The commission may order a compliance proceeding to determine

                   the final amounts of over-recovery that must be refunded to

                   customers and the form timing of the refund.

H.         Large load customer interconnection fee and financial security

           1.      Remove overlap with large load interconnection rule

           Proposed §25.192(k) overlaps with the Commission’s separately proposed rule in Project

No. 58481 regarding large load interconnections that will govern the various aspects of large load

interconnections on the ERCOT system.30 The Proposal for Publication in Project No. 58481

includes provisions related to interconnection fees and financial security.31 To avoid conflicting

language on the same topics covered in different rules, TEC recommends deleting subsection (k)

from this PFP in its entirety.32

           2.      Protect the tax-exempt status of electric cooperatives

           If subsection (k) remains in this rule, it must be adjusted to account for the tax-exempt

status of electric cooperatives. Electric cooperatives operate as private not-for-profit entities for

federal tax purposes. To maintain this tax-exempt status, electric cooperatives must receive at least

85% of their annual income from members.33 This is often referred to as the 85/15 Rule.

Proposal for Publication of New 16 TAC §25.194 (Mar. 12, 2026).

            Proposed §25.192(k)(1) and (k)(2) indicate that interconnection fee payments and

forfeitures of financial security must be made directly from a large load customer to a TSP.34

Generation and transmission (G&T) electric cooperatives typically serve as TSPs and are usually

comprised of member electric cooperatives that are DSPs. G&Ts are not certificated to provide

retail service, rather their member DSPs are. For this reason, large load customers do not receive

retail electric service directly from a G&T TSP, and the large load customers are not “members”

of the G&T TSP. In most cases, in non-competitive areas involving a G&T, the provision of retail

electric service is sleeved through or facilitated by a DSP member cooperative that is certificated

to provide retail service to the location of the large load. The large load customer is a member of

the DSP cooperative. Through this arrangement, the large load customer makes payments to the

DSP cooperative of which it is a member, and the DSP cooperative remits payment to the G&T

TSP as a member of that G&T cooperative. This structure allows the G&T TSP to remain

                                  II.    General Comments

       TEC's member cooperatives represent a diverse set of load profiles across the state, with

varying degrees of traditional industrial load, computational large load, and smaller residential or

commercial loads. Because of these different profiles, moving from a 4 coincident peak (CP)

determinant with fifteen-minute intervals to a 12CP determinant with thirty-minute intervals will

impact TEC' s member cooperatives in different ways. TEC, therefore, takes no position on the

transition to a 12CP methodology with thirty-minute intervals. An increased number of CPs and

increased interval length may lessen the likelihood that large load consumers can avoid

transmission costs but may increase costs for some TEC members. Efficient market signals are

vital to maintaining appropriate levels of generation and transmission buildout. Ultimately,

regardless of the methodology chosen, whether that be a set number of CPs, net CPs, or total

system usage, the Commission should endeavor to adopt a methodology that minimizes distortions

to the energy market.

should continue to periodically monitor transmission cost allocation as more sophisticated users

adjust to the new CP regime, increasing their ability to potentially avoid CPs and shift costs onto

other consumers.
